source.title: A Solvable Model of Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: A. Maloney; Daniel A. Roberts; J. Sully

record.tranche_reason: The study develops and analyzes a solvable random-feature regression model, then compares its test-loss scaling with the scaling-law claim. It is a conceptual test, not a reproduction on language models.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses empirical LLM scaling results and compute-optimal training from cited work, but those are not new results here. Its own results concern random-feature linear regression and toy or synthetic data; it also reports an image classification comparison. It does not measure cross-entropy on language models or run a small-run-to-large-run prediction experiment.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a solvable random-feature linear regression model with simulations. Its toy-model test MSE is not language-model pretraining loss, so those rows do not bear on V1–V4, V6 or V7. The one result on a real dataset is a random ReLU-feature regression on MNIST 7-vs-9 (§4.4, Fig. 14). It shows a power-law test-loss falloff with training-set size, a new-setting result for V5 (image modality).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also argue the following. Equiparameterization (N∝T) is optimal for regularized generalized linear models, which they say is consistent with Hoffmann et al. Double descent is an artefact of the ridgeless limit. Their synthetic data model, unlike MNIST, fails to extend the loss power law through a ReLU map.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a generative latent-data model, random features, and generalized linear regression with MSE and ridge regularization, rather than autoregressive transformer pretraining with held-out cross-entropy. It analyzes an effectively infinite-compute optimum.
record.method_sensitivity: The results depend on the latent-space size M, whether the model is ridgeless or optimally regularized, whether the data spectrum is power-law or Marchenko–Pastur, and whether features are mapped through a ReLU layer.

fits_no_version.finding: An optimally regularized random-feature regression on power-law latent data reproduces power-law and plateau behaviour, with L∝(1/N+1/T)^α and equal exponents (Figs. 7–8, Eqs. 163–171).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law data spectra plus a spectrum-extending feature map suffice to produce scaling-law loss behaviour in solvable models.

fits_no_version.finding: When N or T exceeds the latent dimension M, the noiseless loss drops to zero; with label noise it falls as roughly 1/T. A fit including M matches simulations where the M-free fit fails (Figs. 8–10, Eqs. 172, 182–188).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A finite latent-space size can bend scaling curves away from a single power law at large scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Plain linear models lack the full phenomenology: isotropic data gives no power law, and power-law data gives no plateau, with loss growing in N (App. A, Figs. 15–16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-law behaviour requires structured data and a separation between model features and data latent features.

fits_no_version.finding: A random ReLU map extends the spectral power law but slightly lowers its exponent. With the synthetic data model, test loss plateaus at Nin rather than continuing (Figs. 4, 13, 14 left).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonlinear feature maps set the loss exponent through how they transform the data spectrum.

record.problems: The evidence is mainly a theoretical statistical model and numerical simulations, not language-model experiments. The measured loss is MSE rather than pretraining cross-entropy; several plotted comparisons provide no numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The image-task comparison is simplified and uses a random-feature model.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant own results left out.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss is measured.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation; the analysis is effectively at infinite compute.
Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are untested. Scaling in parameters or features on natural images is untested (only T is varied on MNIST). Trained neural networks are untested.
No downstream tasks are related to scale or to pretraining loss.
No fits to real model runs and no comparison of published laws or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: This is essentially a theory paper. Its simulations are of a toy model, which is not the kind of system named in V1–V4, V6 or V7, so most rows are relinked to none and recorded under fits_no_version. The reader's V1 supports/limits/challenges labels and V7 limits_scope label are dropped for that reason. r9 is removed from V6. The only empirical natural-data loss result is the MNIST 7-vs-9 curve, which is rescaled, figure-only and covers a single dataset.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy measurements on language models; results concern test MSE in statistical and toy models.
No power-law fitted on small runs is used to predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
The analysis is effectively in the infinite-compute limit and does not measure parameter and token counts as functions of a fixed compute budget.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Image data are considered, including a simplified MNIST task; video, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
The downstream-style result is limited to a simplified MNIST 7-versus-9 task; the study does not relate downstream performance to language-model pretraining loss or test language-model benchmarks.
No language-model fit is performed, and the study does not independently compare the published Kaplan and Hoffmann exponents; cited results are not new evidence.

rows.subject: joint statistical model (random-feature linear regression)
rows.stage_stated: ridgeless limit; also discussed with optimized ridge parameter
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate test loss as resources approach or exceed the latent-space size

conditions.value: T approaches M with N much larger than T and M

rows.value: As T approaches M from below, the loss tends to zero; for T > M the stated noiseless large-N loss is zero.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a breakdown of the ordinary scaling-law fit at finite latent-space size.
rows.check: Breakdown when T approaches latent size M is a toy-model prediction. The authors say LLMs have not yet shown finite-M effects. The behaviour it describes (loss to zero as T→M) occurs fully, so 'partial' is not the right state.

rows.subject: joint statistical model (random-feature linear regression)
rows.size_stated: N features and T training samples
rows.operation_detail: Compare test loss under joint scaling of features and training-set size

conditions.value: large relative to N and T

rows.value: The model has equal scaling exponents for N and T; N(T) = T avoids the plateau in this model.
rows.note: This allocation is between features and samples, not a measured fixed-compute optimum.
rows.check: Equal N and T exponents and N=T optimality concern features versus samples in an infinite-compute toy model. No fixed-compute optimum is measured, so it does not bear on V3 or on V7's fitting-choice dependence.

rows.subject: joint statistical model (random-feature linear regression)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the original phenomenological fit with a fit that includes latent-space size
rows.note: The text says the fit without M departs from simulations as N approaches M, while the M-dependent fit continues to fit closely.
rows.check: Comparison of a fit with and without M, in toy-model simulations only. Fig. 8 bottom right shows the M-free fit diverging as N approaches M.

rows.subject: linear model trained on Marchenko–Pastur data
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss while varying training-set size and feature count
rows.value: The study states that this model does not have power-law scaling; for T > N the loss contribution is noise, and for T < N the signal term decreases as 1 − T/N.
rows.note: Used as a simpler-data control to show that unstructured data does not produce the scaling-law behavior.
rows.check: Linear model on isotropic (Marchenko–Pastur) data, used as a toy control. Not a language model.

rows.subject: linear model trained on power-law data
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss against training-set size
rows.value: For T much smaller than N, the loss scales as T^-α; the study states there is no plateau behavior for T > N.
rows.note: This simpler linear model lacks the full two-resource behavior of the joint random-feature model.
rows.check: Linear model on power-law data without a feature map; a toy comparator.

rows.subject: linear model trained on power-law data
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss while varying feature count
rows.value: The study describes the loss as growing with N in this regime.
rows.note: The authors attribute this behavior to the linear model also increasing the complexity of the labels with N.
rows.check: Loss grows with N because the label complexity grows with N by construction (Fig. 16 top right). This is a toy artefact and cannot challenge V1.

rows.subject: MNIST 7-versus-9 simplified classification task
rows.size_stated: input dimension Nin = 784; ReLU network width N = 20000
rows.stage_stated: random-feature ReLU network followed by linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss as the training-set size increases
rows.note: The text says the natural-image task continues to show power-law loss falloff beyond Nin; the plot is rescaled for comparison and the exponent was chosen to match the model-data curve.
rows.check: Not V6: it is test MSE versus training-set size on one image task, not downstream performance versus pretraining scale or loss. The value is figure-only. The MNIST loss is rescaled, and the comparison model's exponent was chosen to match MNIST. Maximum T is 12,214.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 and MNIST feature representations under a random ReLU map
rows.size_stated: input dimensions stated as Nin = 3072 for CIFAR-10 and Nin = 784 for MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Compare power-law spectral fits before and after the ReLU feature map
rows.measure: power-law exponent of the feature spectrum
rows.value: The study states that the fitted exponent α decreases slightly after the ReLU map.
rows.note: The authors say this exponent ultimately characterizes the test-loss power law, but the plotted result here is a spectral measurement, not a separate loss measurement.
rows.check: Measures the feature-spectrum exponent, not test loss, so it bears on no version. The slight decrease in α after ReLU is stated in the text (footnote 18, §4.4).

relationships.condition: MNIST 7-vs-9, random ReLU features (width 20000) plus linear regression, T up to 12,214
relationships.reason: Fig. 14 right shows MNIST test loss following a power-law falloff in T past Nin=784 (r9). The evidence is figure-only, with the loss rescaled.
relationships.display_finding: Rescaled test loss showed a power-law decline as training-set size increased beyond the input dimension of 784.
